M E T A B O L I S M
Loss of FTO in adipose tissue decreases Angptl4
translation and alters triglyceride metabolism
Chao-Yung Wang,1* Shian-Sen Shie,2 Ming-Shien Wen,1 Kuo-Chun Hung,1 I-Chang Hsieh,1
Ta-Sen Yeh,3 Delon Wu1
A common variant of the FTO (fat mass– and obesity-associated) gene is a risk factor for obesity. We
found that mice with an adipocyte-specific deletion of FTO gained more weight than control mice on a
high-fat diet. Analysis of mice lacking FTO in adipocytes fed a normal diet or adipocytes from these mice
revealed alterations in triglyceride metabolism that would be expected to favor increased fatty acid stor-
age by adipose tissue. Mice lacking FTO in adipocytes showed increased serum triglyceride breakdown
and clearance, which was associated with lower serum triglyceride concentrations. In addition, lipolysis
in response to b-adrenergic stimulation was decreased in adipocytes and ex vivo adipose explants from
the mutant mice. FTO is a nucleic acid demethylase that removes N6-methyladenosine (m6A) from
mRNAs. We found that FTO bound to Angptl4, which encodes an adipokine that stimulates intracellular
lipolysis in adipocytes. Unexpectedly, the adipose tissue of fasted or fed mice lacking FTO in adipocytes
had greater Angptl4 mRNA abundance. However, after high-fat feeding, the mutant mice had less
Angptl4 protein and more m6A-modified Angptl4 than control mice, suggesting that lack of FTO prevented
the translation of Angptl4. Injection of Angptl4-encoding adenovirus into mice lacking FTO in adipocytes
restored serum triglyceride concentrations and lipolysis to values similar to those in control mice and
abolished excessive weight gain from a high-fat diet. These results reveal that FTO regulates fatty acid
mobilization in adipocytes and thus body weight in part through posttranscriptional regulation of Angptl4.
INTRODUCTION
Obesity is an important public health problem. It predisposes individuals
to numerous diseases, including ischemic heart disease, hypertension, dia-
betes mellitus, and cerebrovascular accidents (1). Single-nucleotide poly-
morphisms rs9939609 in intron 1 of the fat mass– and obesity-associated
(FTO) gene are associated with an increased risk of adult obesity (2) in
different ethnic groups worldwide (3). About 16% of individuals of
European descent are homozygous for the risk allele and weigh on aver-
age ~3 kg more than those with the protective allele (4). A meta-analysis
of genome-wide association studies with a sample size of ~170,000 in
body mass index in a human population has shown that rs7202116 at
the FTO locus is associated with phenotypic variability and no foci other
than FTO have significant effects on body mass index variability (5). Al-
though these FTO polymorphisms do not directly affect FTO functions,
they regulate IRX3 expression and RPGRIP1L (6–8). The exact role of
FTO in human obesity remains unclear.
Food intake can be altered by manipulation of FTO mRNA expression
in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (9). Enhanced FTO expression in
mice leads to hyperphagia, increased fat mass, and higher body weight
(10, 11). Mice with a neuronal-specific deletion of FTO have an identical
lean body weight phenotype to mice with a global FTO deletion (12). FTO
is found in almost every cell and tissue type and is most likely located in the
nucleus owing to a nuclear localization sequence. It is a 2-oxoglutarate–
dependent nucleic acid demethylase (13) and has efficient oxidative de-
methylation activity that targets the abundant N6-methyladenosine (m6A)
residues in mRNA (14). Cells lacking FTO display decreased activation of
the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 pathway, decreased mRNA
translation rates, and increased autophagy (15). FTO also modulates CBP
[cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) response element–binding pro-
tein] signaling by interacting with calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein
kinase II (16). These findings suggest that the effect of FTO on body weight
could be determined by its cellular functions. FTO deficiency may result
in multiple organ abnormalities in humans. Loss-of-function mutations in
FTO have been detected in a large Palestinian Arab multiplex family, which
result in postnatal growth retardation, microcephaly, severe psychomotor
delay, functional brain deficits, and characteristic facial dysmorphism
(17). Furthermore, homozygous FTO knockout mice demonstrate post-
natal growth retardation and a significant reduction in adipose tissue
and lean body mass (18).
Adipose tissue plays important roles in the development of obesity
(19, 20). Adipocytes with FTO deficiency have increased uncoupling
protein 1 (UCP-1) abundance and mitochondrial uncoupling in vitro (21).
On the basis of this evidence, we hypothesized that FTO plays a critical
role in adipose tissue functions and alters energy homeostasis.
RESULTS
High-fat diet increases the abundance of FTO at the
mRNA and protein levels in adipose tissue
FTO was present in the subcutaneous fat, visceral fat, and brown fat of
mice (fig. S1). In mice fed a high-fat diet for 2 or 14 days, the abundance
of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor g (PPAR-g) increased (fig.
S2, A and B), as reported previously (22), and FTO abundance at the
mRNA and protein levels remained unaltered in brown fat but increased
in subcutaneous and visceral fat (fig. S2, A and B), an effect that was
prevented by the PPAR-g inhibitor GW9662 (fig. S2, C and D). Increased
adipose FTO abundance after short-term high-fat diet, which was used
to test the effect of high-fat diet without the interference of obesity and

that FTO in adipose tissue could have a physiological role in
response to this dietary challenge. Mice with global FTO dele-
tion have higher postnatal mortality rates and postnatal growth
retardation, thus rendering these mice unsuitable for studying
energy homeostasis and the role of FTO in adipose tissue (23).
To delete FTO specifically in adipocytes, we bred mice with a
conditional FTO allele with mice expressing Cre recombinase
under the control of an adipocyte-specific promoter of the adipo-
nectin gene. We used littermate male mice homozygous for the
FTO conditional allele without Cre recombinase as controls
(FTOf/f; wild-type mice) for mice with adipocyte-specific FTO
deletion [Adiponectin-Cre FTOf/f (AFO mice); fig. S3A]. In AFO
mice, which were born at the expected Mendelian ratio, Cre re-
combinase led to successful knockout of FTO in white and
brown adipocytes, respectively (fig. S3B). FTO protein was al-
most absent in white and brown adipocytes of AFO mice (fig.
S3C). FTO deletion was not detected in macrophages, brain, liver,
muscle, and heart (fig. S3, B and C).
AFO mice gain more weight on a high-fat diet
We fed AFO and wild-type mice with chow diet or high-fat diet
starting at 6 weeks of age. AFO mice were born with a normal
weight and had similar body weight gain on chow diet compared
to that observed in wild-type mice (Fig. 1, A and B). High-fat
diet–fed AFO mice gained significantly more weight than did
wild-type mice (Fig. 1, A and B), which is notable because the
Adiponectin-Cre control mice gained less body weight and ex-
pended more energy than C57BL/6J mice (fig. S4A). Magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) revealed that AFO mice had more
body fat, with similar amounts of lean body mass (Fig. 1C). Con-
sistent with MRI data, visceral and subcutaneous fat depot weights
were increased in high-fat diet–fed AFO mice (Fig. 1D). Tibial
lengths and weights of heart, kidney, muscle, and brain tissues
were similar in AFO and wild-type mice. However, compared to
wild-type mice, the livers of AFO mice weighed more and had a
fatty appearance (Fig. 1D). Histological analysis revealed adipo-
cyte hypertrophy in AFO mice (Fig. 1E). Furthermore, brown fat
showed more lipid deposition and had a white fat–like appearance
(Fig. 1F), and adipocytes were larger in AFO mice than in wild-
type mice after high-fat diet (Fig. 1G). Significantly less mito-
chondrial DNA was detected in brown fat from AFO mice than
in that from wild-type mice (Fig. 1H).
To characterize energy homeostasis in AFO mice, we per-
formed indirect calorimetry on 8-week-old mice after 2 weeks
on a high-fat diet, before the body weights of AFO and wild-type
mice significantly differed. Respiratory O2 consumption indicated
that AFO mice expended less energy than wild-type mice in light
and dark phases (Fig. 2A). Food intake did not differ significant-
ly between the two groups fed a high-fat diet between 6 and
19 weeks of age (Fig. 2B). Activity in AFO mice was reduced
only during the light phase, whereas O2 consumption rate (VO2)
was reduced both in light and dark phases (Fig. 2, C and D).
Although carbon dioxide output and resting energy require-
ments were significantly reduced in both light and dark phases
(Fig. 2, E and F), analysis of covariance (ANCOVA)–adjusted
analysis indicated that energy expenditure was only significantly
reduced during light phases (Fig. 2G). Thyroid function was simi-
lar in AFO and wild-type mice (fig. S4B). We performed
paired feeding experiments to delineate whether the effect of

diet. Feeding AFO and wild-type mice the same number of calories on
either a chow diet or a high-fat diet revealed that AFO mice on the high-fat
diet still gained more body weight than wild-type mice (fig. S4C). These
results indicated that the greater weight gain of AFO mice on a high-fat
diet was because of greater adipose tissue mass and reduced energy
expenditure. Analysis of brown fat from AFO mice revealed
decreased expression of PGC1-a (which encodes peroxisome
proliferator–activated receptor-g coactivator 1a), UCP-1,
Dio2 (which encodes type II iodothyronine deiodinase), and
CIDEA (which encodes cell death–inducing DNA fragmen-
tation factor–like effector A) compared to wild-type mice,
but no differences in the expression of TFAM (which encodes
mitochondrial transcription factor A), BMP7 (which encodes
bone morphogenetic protein 7), NRF1 (which encodes nuclear
respiratory factor 1), and PRDM16 (which encodes PR domain–
containing 16) (fig. S5).
Because obesity and increased adipose tissue mass disrupt
glucose metabolism (24), we assessed glucose and insulin ho-
meostasis in AFO mice. AFO and wild-type mice fed a normal
chow diet had similar basal blood glucose and insulin concen-
trations, glucose tolerance, and insulin sensitivities (Fig. 2H and
fig. S6, A and B). However, AFO mice fed a high-fat diet devel-
oped glucose intolerance and impaired insulin sensitivity (Fig.
2, I and J) and had higher basal blood insulin concentrations
than wild-type mice (Fig. 2J). Compared with wild-type mice,
AFO mice fed a high-fat diet showed similar plasma adiponectin
concentrations but significantly higher leptin concentrations (Fig.
2, K and L). FTO suppresses the phosphorylation of STAT3 (sig-
nal transducer and activator of transcription 3) induced by leptin
(23), and greater plasma leptin concentrations might be corre-
lated with greater adipose tissue mass in AFO mice or result di-
rectly from FTO deficiency in adipocytes (25).
Consistent with their obesity and insulin resistance, 20-week-
old AFO mice fed a high-fat diet had increased serum-free fatty
acid and triglyceride concentrations (Fig. 2, J and M). Serum-
free fatty acid is regulated by fat mass, lipolysis, free fatty acid
metabolism, and insulin resistance (26). However, age-matched
chow diet–fed AFO mice had significantly lower triglyceride con-
centrations but increased serum-free fatty acid concentrations.
Eight-week-old AFO mice fed either a chow diet or high-fat diet
exhibited decreased triglyceride but similar serum-free fatty acid
concentrations. Total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL),
and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) did not significantly differ
between AFO and wild-type mice (Fig. 2M).
Intracellular lipolysis is impaired in AFO mice on a
normal diet and in adipocytes from AFO mice, and
triglyceride clearance is accelerated in AFO mice
We were intrigued that AFO mice gained weight after a high-fat
diet but had lower triglyceride concentrations on a chow diet, im-
plying altered adipocyte function and lipid homeostasis. In line
with this notion, metabolomics analysis of epididymal adipose
tissue from AFO and wild-type mice revealed increased saturated
and unsaturated fatty acid concentrations in AFO mice (fig. S7).
However, the lack of FTO protein (fig. S8) did not appear to alter
the differentiation of primary preadipocytes from AFO mice into
mature adipocytes (Fig 3A). After insulin stimulation, AFO adipo-
cytes took up more glucose (Fig. 3B), leading us to perform lipo-
genesis assays with lipidomics analysis (Fig. 3C) to measure the
metabolism of glucose into fatty acids. After insulin stimulation, AFO adipo-
cytes synthesized more saturated fatty acids (Fig. 3C) but less unsaturated
fatty acids than wild-type adipocytes (Fig. 3C). Specifically, the concentra-
tions of arachidonic acid (C 20:4) and eicosapentaenoic acid (C 20:5) were
lower in AFO adipocytes than in wild-type adipocytes. Because AFO adipo-

S9, A to D), altered intracellular lipolysis and/
or enhanced de novo lipogenesis could be the
basis for the increased adipocyte hypertrophy
in AFO mice. Although increased glucose
uptake and lipogenesis in AFO adipocytes
would be consistent with the increases in
adipocyte size and body weight after high-
fat diet feeding in AFO mice, these changes
would not explain the lower triglyceride con-
centrations in AFO mice on a chow diet. We
next examined whether altered lipolysis caused
adipocyte hypertrophy and altered triglyceride
concentrations. Lipolysis was significantly
lower in mature adipocytes from in vitro
differentiated FTO knockout preadipocytes
than in wild-type adipocytes (Fig. 3D). Further-
more, intraperitoneal injection of the b-adrenergic
agonist isoproterenol failed to significantly stim-
ulate the in vivo lipolysis rate in AFO mice
(Fig. 3E). We also confirmed that the b3-
adrenoceptor agonist BRL37344 failed to
stimulate lipolysis in primary AFO adipocytes
(Fig. 3F). Net in vivo lipolytic rates as calcu-
lated from the absolute rate of new triacylglyc-
erol synthesis and the change in adipose
tissue mass were also decreased in AFO mice
(Fig. 3G). From these results, we concluded
that lipolysis in AFO mice was reduced.
The lower fasting triglyceride concentra-
tions in AFO mice could also result from de-
creased plasma triglyceride excursion, which
comprises three components: fasting triglyceride,
postprandial elevation of triglyceride, and tri-
glyceride clearance (27). Oral fat tolerance tests
revealed that in addition to lower fasting tri-
glyceride concentrations, AFO mice showed re-
duced triglyceride excursion after oral gavage
with olive oil (Fig. 4A). We ruled out decreased
plasma entry of triglycerides as the mechanism
underlying the decreased plasma triglyceride
excursion because treatment of AFO mice
with poloxamer 407 to inhibit triglyceride
clearance before olive oil loading resulted
in triglyceride accumulation rates that were
similar to those in wild-type mice (Fig. 4B).
Intraperitoneal triglyceride loading, which by-
passes gut absorption, confirmed that AFO
mice had an increased triglyceride clearance
rate (Fig. 4C). Moreover, AFO and wild-type
mice extracted similar percentages of dietary
triglyceride extracted from diet (Fig. 4D). Tri-
glyceride clearance requires the enzyme LPL,
which hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons
and very low density lipoproteins into free
fatty acids and monoacylglycerol molecules
(28) and is distributed in adipose tissue and
cardiac and skeletal muscles (29). LPL is

FTO binds to and demethylates Angptl4 mRNA, leading
to decreased translation of Angptl4
We reasoned that FTO-deficient adipose tissue might result in altered adi-
pokine secretion that substantially affected postheparin LPL activity. To
identify targets of FTO in adipose tissue, we performed RNA immuno-
precipitation and RNA sequencing in transgenic mice that globally express
Flag-FTO driven by the CAG promoter (fig. S10A). After normalization
and enrichment analysis between Flag and immunoglobulin G (IgG) im-
munoprecipitates, we cross-referenced the 31 enriched RNA targets that
were related to lipid homeostasis with microarray data from wild-type
and AFO adipose tissue (fig. S10, B to D). We analyzed the expression
data and used quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) to
compare the expression of genes involved in lipolytic pathways in adipose
tissue from AFO and wild-type mice under fed or fasting conditions (Fig.
4G and fig. S11). Angiopoietin-like 4 (Angptl4) is an adipokine that in-
hibits LPL and also stimulates intracellular lipolysis in adipocytes (31),
and we found that Angptl4 RNA immunoprecipitated with Flag-FTO (fig.
S10D). Fed or fasted AFO mice had significantly greater expression of
Angptl4 mRNA than wild-type mice (Fig. 4G).
Increased Angptl4 mRNA abundance implied that Angptl4
might contribute to the impaired lipolysis in AFO mice (31–33).
However, the reported inhibition of LPL by Angptl4 (34) is in-
consistent with our observations of increased Angptl4 mRNA
abundance and increased LPL activity in AFO mice. Thus, we
analyzed the protein abundance of Angptl4 in adipose tissue
in mice on different diets. In response to 2 days of high-fat diet,
a dietary challenge that would be expected to increase Angptl4
amounts, the protein abundance of Angptl4 in adipose tissue
increased to a lesser extent in AFO mice than in wild-type mice
(Fig. 5A). Furthermore, serum Angptl4 concentrations increased
significantly in wild-type mice, but not in AFO mice, whereas
serum concentrations of Angptl3 were similar between wild-type
and AFO mice (Fig. 5B). The PPAR-g agonist rosiglitazone in-
creases Angptl4 abundance through a PPAR response element in
the Angptl4 promoter (35). Rosiglitazone dose-dependently stim-
ulated increases in Angptl4 abundance in wild-type adipose tis-
sue explants but not in those from AFO mice (Fig. 5C). However,
rosiglitazone increased Angptl4 mRNA abundance in a dose-
dependent manner in primary adipocytes from both wild-type
and AFO mice, with significantly greater amounts of Angptl4
mRNA in AFO adipocytes (Fig. 5D). Because FTO is an m6A
demethylase (13) and because m6A modification of mRNA
regulates RNA stability and export (36, 37), we hypothesized
that FTO-mediated regulation of Angptl4 was most likely at
the posttranscriptional level. We found that FTO directly bound to
Angptl4 mRNA (Fig. 5E) at both the 5′ and 3′ untranslated regions
(UTRs) of Angptl4 mRNA as determined by RNA electrophoret-
ic mobility shift assays (EMSAs) (fig. S12, A to C). m6A
immunoprecipitation assays revealed a higher percentage of
m6A-modified Angptl4 mRNA in the adipose tissue of AFO
mice (Fig. 5F), suggesting that FTO removed the m6A modifi-
cation from Angptl4 mRNA. After 2 days of high-fat diet, the
percentage of m6A-modified Angptl4 mRNA decreased in
wild-type mice but not in AFO mice (Fig. 5F). Furthermore,
treatment of AFO adipocytes with 3-deazaadenosine (DAA),
an inhibitor of m6A methylation, partially reversed the discrep-
ancy between Angptl4 mRNA and protein abundance (fig. S13, A to C).
This finding was consistent with the m6A modification at the 5′UTR and
3′UTR of Angptl4 mRNA as determined by m6A immunoprecipitation
and RNA sequencing (fig. S14). These results suggest that FTO regulates
Angptl4 abundance by binding to and m6A demethylating the mRNA
for this protein.
To further investigate the mechanism underlying the discrepancy be-
tween the Angptl4 mRNA and protein abundance, we quantified Angptl4
transcripts in nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions in wild-type and AFO
mice. We found that the increased Angptl4 mRNA was mainly in the cy-
toplasm and there was no significant difference in the nuclear amounts of
Angptl4, LPL, or GAPDH mRNA (Fig. 5G). Polysome profiling revealed
that the average polysome size was lower in AFO adipocytes than in wild-
type adipocytes, indicating that less mRNA, including Angptl4, was being
translated (Fig. 5H). Further examination of the Angptl4 mRNA profiles
showed that the abundance of Angptl4 mRNA in the polysome fraction
was lower in AFO adipocytes than in wild-type adipocytes (Fig. 5I). Sim-
ilarly, there was less Angptl4 mRNA in the polysome fraction of MCF-7
human breast cancer cells with stable FTO knockdown (fig. S15, A and
B). We also noticed a similar mRNA shift pattern in LPL mRNA, but the
decrease in LPL in the polysome fractions in AFO adipocytes was less
substantial than that of Angptl4, suggesting that FTO knockout in adipo-
cytes had gene-specific effects.

Angptl4 is required for the regulation of lipolysis
in adipocytes by FTO and rescues the obesity
and impaired lipolysis phenotype of AFO mice
We explored whether Angptl4 was essential for FTO-regulated
lipolysis in adipocytes. Infection of adenovirus encoding FTO
resulted in significant inhibition of LPL activity in wild-type adi-
pocytes but not in adipocytes from Angptl4-deficient mice (Fig.
6A). Moreover, knockdown of FTO did not affect LPL activity in
Angptl4 knockout adipocytes but significantly increased LPL ac-
tivity in wild-type adipocytes (Fig. 6B). In line with previous ob-
servations, knockdown or overexpression of FTO significantly
alteredlipolysis inwild-type adipocytes inthepresenceor absence
of b3-adrenoceptor stimulation with BRL37344 but not in adipo-
cytes deficient in Angptl4 (Fig. 6, C and D). Application of puri-
fied Angptl4 or adenovirus expressing Angptl4 rescued the
impaired lipolysis in AFO adipocytes (Fig. 6, E and F).
To determine whether the decreased Angptl4 abundance
caused the increased body weight in AFO mice, we injected an
adenovirus expressing Angptl4 into the inguinal fat pads, which
comprises ~40% of whole-body white adipose tissue of young
adult mice (38), of AFO mice. The abundance of Angptl4 in
AFO inguinal fat pads was similar to that in wild-type ingui-
nal fat pads 2 weeks after injection (fig. S16, A and B). AFO
mice that received Angptl4 adenovirus had normal serum tri-
glyceride concentrations, whereas AFO mice that received con-
trol adenovirus had lower serum triglyceride concentrations
(fig. S16C). After high-fat diet feeding, 7-week-old wild-type
and AFO mice were injected with control or Angptl4 virus
in the inguinal fat pad. Consistent with the hypothesis that
lower Angptl4 abundance in adipose tissue in AFO mice
was responsible for the increase in body weight, AFO mice
injected with Angptl4 virus gained a similar amount of body
weight as wild-type mice (Fig. 6G). In vivo lipolysis after iso-
proterenol stimulation was similar in AFO mice receiving
Angptl4 adenovirus and wild-type mice (Fig. 6H). These find-
ings indicated that increasing Angptl4 abundance in adipose
tissue restored body weight, triglyceride concentrations, and li-
polysis in AFO mice.
DISCUSSION
Deficiency of FTO specifically in adipose tissue resulted in im-
paired lipolysis, accelerated triglyceride clearance, and obesity
after high-fat diet feeding through modulation of Angptl4 tran-
scription. Our observation that adipose FTO deficiency predisposed
mice to increased body weight differs from previous studies per-
formed on FTO-deficient mice. Global FTO knockout (18) or
FTO C-terminal mutation mice (39) exhibit reduced body weight,
a complex phenotype that is the result of increased energy ex-
penditure, increased sympathetic activity, and decreased food
intake. The complexity of the phenotype that results from global
FTO deficiency and the high embryonic lethality suggest the
importance of FTO in multiple organ systems. Deletion of FTO
in adult mice, which bypasses the detrimental effects of FTO
deficiency during development, results in increased fat mass
without altering energy expenditure, which is compatible with
our findings in AFO mice (20). Moreover, our findings con-
firm that decreased fat mass in mice with global FTO deficiency
is not due to defective adipose tissue development because
chow-fed AFO mice had normal fat mass.

Consistent with the increased sympathetic activity and energy expend-
iture phenotype in global FTO knockout mice, previous reports showed
that adipocytes from global FTO–deficient mice exhibited increased UCP-
1 and mitochondrial uncoupling (18). However, brown fat in AFO mice
had a phenotype more reminiscent of white fat (Fig. 1F). We believe that
this difference was due to the influence of global FTO knockout in other
organs, such as skeletal muscle. Skeletal muscle through secreted myo-
kines can transform white fat into beige fat and modulate thermogenesis
(40, 41). Global FTO knockout mice could have altered myokine secre-
tion, which results in a different composition of fat cell types from AFO
mice. We believe that future studies with mice with skeletal muscle–specific
knockout of FTO will help to clarify this discrepancy.
Our results showed that AFO mice had lower Angptl4 abundance in ad-
ipose tissue. Like AFO mice, Angptl4-deficient mice also exhibit increased
body weight (42), lower triglyceride concentrations, and impaired lipolysis
(31). However, there are several differences between Angptl4-deficient mice
and AFO mice. First, Angptl4-deficient mice develop severe fibrinopurulent
peritonitis when fed saturated fat (29), whereas AFO mice, even after
5 months on a high-fat diet, did not develop peritonitis. Second, food intake
is altered in Angptl4-deficient mice (35), but AFO mice had similar food
intake to wild-type mice. We believe that these differences are due to
Angptl4-deficient mice lacking Angptl4 globally and constitutively and
AFO mice not producing Angptl4 in response to the appropriate stimuli, such
as starvation, free fatty acids, and rosiglitazone. Although baseline Angptl4
abundance in adipose tissue was lower in AFO mice, serum Angptl4 con-
centrations and LPL activity were significantly different after fasting or
stimulation with rosiglitazone or free fatty acids. Our results implied that
the role of FTO in Angptl4 expression was mainly to regulate its translation
in response to stimulation. Angptl4 inhibits extracellular lipolysis by inhibit-
ing LPL (43) and stimulates intracellular lipolysis in adipocytes (31). Our
results indicated that FTO deficiency affects intracellular Angptl4 produc-
tion and intracellular lipolysis (Fig. 7). Future studies will be necessary to
determine whether FTO affects Angptl4-mediated regulation of extra-
cellular lipolysis (31), a process that is required for triglyceride clearance.

mitotic clonal expansion (45) in global FTO-deficient mice. AFO mice
were created with Adiponectin-Cre mice (46). The Cre recombination of
FTO alleles occurred at a late stage of embryogenesis (47) and enabled us
to study FTO function in mature adipocytes. Indeed, FTO heterozygous
deleted mice gained more subcutaneous fat mass than wild-type mice
when placed on a high-fat diet (48). This result and our data both imply
that FTO has important functions in mature adipocytes and deficiency of
FTO in mature adipocyte increases fat mass.
In conclusion, our results identify FTO-dependent regulation of Angptl4
as an endogenous mechanism that allows adipose tissue to adapt its me-
tabolism in response to environmental or nutritional changes. Future chal-
lenges will involve understanding the regulatory mechanisms by which food
or starvation affect m6A modifications in adipose mRNA, as well as de-
fining therapeutic approaches to alter these modifications in adipose tissue
in diabetes or obesity.

RNA EMSA
In vitro transcribed Angptl4 RNAs (MEGAscript Kit, Ambion) were end-
labeled with biotin according to the manufacturer’s protocol (RNA 3′ End
Biotinylation Kit, Pierce). The 3′-biotinylated RNA and FTO protein (Alexis)
were incubated in binding buffer [10 mM Hepes, 20 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2,
1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), 0.01% NP-40, 5% glycerol, and 0.5 mg of tRNA]
for 30 min at room temperature, with or without excess unlabeled RNA
competitors. For competition with labeled RNA, a 160-fold molar excess
of unlabeled RNA relative to biotin-labeled RNAwas added to the binding
assay. Different segments of Angptl4 mRNA were in vitro transcribed and
incubated with or without FTO protein. FTO protein–Angptl4 mRNA
complexes were analyzed in three groups: free probes (F), FTO protein-
Angptl4 mRNA probe complexes (FTO), and nonlabeled Angptl4 mRNA
competitor + FTO protein–Angptl4 mRNA probes complexes (C). Reaction
mixtures were resolved on a 6% native polyacrylamide gel, transferred
to positively charged nylon membranes, and cross-linked using a Stratagene
cross-linker. Band shift was visualized with streptavidin-alkaline phos-
phatase through chemoluminescent detection (BrightStar BioDetect Kit,
Ambion).
RNA immunoprecipitation
Transgenic FTO mice were fasted overnight and adipose tissues were lysed
in passive lysis buffer [10 mM Hepes (pH 7.0), 100 mM KCl, 5 mM
MgCl2, and 0.5% NP-40] containing 1 mM DTT, SUPERase In (100 U/ml;
Ambion), and protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche). Homogenates were then
gently lysed with repeated freezing at −80°C and subsequent thawing.
Passive lysis buffer lysates were diluted 10-fold in NET-2 buffer [50 mM
tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM MgCl2, 0.05% NP-40, 20 mM
EDTA (pH 8.0), 1 mM DTT, and SUPERase In (100 U/ml)], precleared
with protein G beads, and immunoprecipitated with antibody specific to
Flag M2 agarose (Sigma) or IgG for 90 min. The agarose was washed six
times with cold NT-2 buffer [50 mM tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl,
1 mM MgCl2, and 1% NP-40]. The input and beads were resuspended in
150 ml of proteinase K buffer [NT-2 buffer supplemented with 1% SDS
and proteinase K (1.2 mg/ml)] for 30 min at 55°C. Immunoprecipitated
RNA was extracted by acid phenol/chloroform for further analysis. The
RNA sequencing was performed on an Illumina HiSeq 2000 system at
the National Center for Genome Medicine, Taiwan. The data were then
transferred to the BioIT group at the National Center for Genome Medicine
for analysis. Analysis consisted of four steps: (i) format conversion and
demultiplexing, (ii) quality check, (iii) sequence alignment using Bowtie,
and (iv) differential expression analysis.
m6A immunoprecipitation analysis
Total RNAwas purified and subjected to treatment with a GenElute mRNA
kit (Sigma). After fragmentation using Ambion RNA Fragmentation Re-
agent (Invitrogen), RNA was immunoprecipitated with anti-m6A antibodies
or IgG coupled to sheep anti-rabbit Dynabeads (Invitrogen) in immuno-
precipitation buffer (10 mM sodium phosphate, 0.05% Triton X, and
140 mM NaCl) (53). After immunoprecipitation, bound RNA and input
RNA were purified with phenol/chloroform extraction and subjected to
qPCR. Immunoprecipitated mRNAs were analyzed by RNA sequencing
and visualized using an integrative genomics viewer. RNA pulled down by
the m6A antibody was normalized to the amount of input RNA to repre-
sent the m6A abundance in individual RNA.

Polysome fraction analysis
Polysomes were isolated from ~2 × 107 wild-type and AFO adipocytes after
cycloheximide (0.1 mg/ml; Sigma) treatment. Cells were lysed with poly-
some lysis buffer (20 mM tris-HCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 100 mM KCl, 1% Tri-

350 ml of polysome extract was layered onto a 7 to 47% sucrose gradient
and centrifuged in Beckman SW 41 Ti rotor at 40,000 rpm for 150 min at
4°C. Gradient fractions were monitored by continuous ultraviolet absorp-
tion at 264 nm, and 18 tubes of ~650-ml fractions were collected. RNA
was purified with PureLink RNA Mini Kit (Ambion).
Adenovirus-mediated gene transfer to mouse
adipose tissues
Incisions (0.5 cm long) were made at the bilateral inguinal area, and mice
received ~30 ml [1 × 109 plaque-forming units (PFU)] of control adenovirus
or adenovirus expressing Angptl4. Lipolysis function and triglyceride
concentrations were assessed 2 weeks after adenovirus injection. For
high-fat diet experiments, our previous experiments had shown that genes
encoded by locally administered adenovirus were expressed for up to
8 weeks. Therefore, we fed wild-type and AFO mice from 6 weeks of age
and injected the adenovirus to subcutaneous adipose tissue at 7 weeks of
age. After adenovirus administration, mice were monitored up to 14 weeks
of age.
Statistical analysis
Animal cohort sizes were determined on the basis of similar previous studies
(54, 55), and no statistical method was used to predetermine sample sizes.
For all high-fat diet feedings, body weight measurement, tissue analysis,
expression analysis, and lipid experiments in mice, the investigators were
blinded to the genotype and sample source during the experiments. Two
AFO mice and their control siblings were excluded from the high-fat diet
experiment and tissue analysis because of insufficient FTO knockout
(<70%) in adipose tissue, as determined by qPCR analysis. One AFO mouse
and control sibling were excluded from the AdAngptl4 injection experi-
ment because of insufficient FTO knockout (<70%) in adipose tissue. For
analysis of all body weight experiments and triglyceride excursion tests,
repeated measures ANOVA was used. For other comparisons, unpaired
Student’s t tests were performed. When comparing energy expenditure, ad-
justments were made for variations in lean mass using multiple linear re-
gression analysis (ANCOVA) (54).
